query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing spark plasma sintering (SPS) of high-purity ZrB2 powder at 1800–1900 °C under ~50–80 MPa and rapid heating (~100 °C/min) with a short dwell (≤10 min) will lower the required densification temperature and reduce residual porosity, mitigating hole formation under prolonged exposure in a liquid plating bath compared to conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2.
generation.material_initial_state: High-purity ZrB2 powder with stoichiometric composition, free of additives or binders.
generation.intervention: Spark plasma sintering at 1800–1900 °C, 50–80 MPa, ~100 °C/min ramp rate, ≤10 min dwell.
generation.conditions: Sintering in vacuum or inert gas at moderate pressure, followed by standard cooling; then extended immersion in a liquid plating bath for service testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Rapid field-assisted heating and applied pressure that enhance mass transport and limit grain growth, yielding dense, defect-minimized microstructures.
generation.mechanism: Localized electrical currents and mechanical pressure accelerate diffusion at lower temperatures, decrease porosity, and increase structural uniformity of single-phase ZrB2, thereby reducing fluid infiltration and hole propagation during plating operations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventional ≥2300 °C sintering, SPS-produced ceramics should exhibit at least 98% density, improved mechanical strength, and substantially fewer plating-induced defects.
generation.baseline: Single-phase ZrB2 consolidated by conventional hot pressing above 2300 °C with longer soak times, typically exhibiting higher porosity and susceptibility to hole formation.
generation.boundary: ZrB2 must remain single-phase, with consistent powder purity and controlled stoichiometry; the SPS process is limited by equipment scale and homogeneity of temperature/pressure distribution.
generation.uncertainty: Despite promising pilot-scale results, large-component uniformity and long-term corrosion data remain limited, requiring further empirical validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of single-phase ZrB2 disks from the same powder lot: one via conventional hot pressing at ~2300 °C for 30 min, the other via SPS at 1800–1900 °C, 50–80 MPa, short dwell ≤10 min. Compare their density, microstructure, and liquid bath infiltration after extended exposure.
measurements: Grain size and porosity analyses by SEM
Infiltration depth and hole formation after ~100 hours submersion in plating solution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If SPS samples do not demonstrate significantly reduced processing temperature, lower porosity, or reduced holes compared with the conventionally sintered group, the hypothesis is invalidated.

The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). It was clear that the distribution of the four Re elements was highly homogeneous without any segregation or aggregation, as shown in Fig. 1g, which implied that the as-synthesized HEReB6-1 nanopowders possessed highly compositional uniformity. Accordingly, it was concluded that highly crystalline single-phase HEReB6-1 nanopowders with high compositional uniformity were synthesized by the solid-state reaction of Re oxides and NaBH4. To remove a small amount of B2O3, the as-synthesized HEReB6-1 nanopowders were first heated in the vacuum furnace at 1,473 K and then sintered into the bulk ceramics by high-pressure sintering at 6 GPa and 1,473–1,773 K. As shown in Fig. S2, there was no change in the phase compositions of HEReB6-1 samples after high-pressure sintering, such as phase separation or transformation. The relative densities and mean grain sizes of the HEReB6-1 samples both tended to increase with increasing sintering temperatures, as presented in Fig. 2a. Specifically, the relative densities and mean grain sizes of the HEReB6-1 samples increased from 74.4% to 97.4% and from 68 ± 32 nm to 145 ± 35 nm, respectively, as the sintering temperatures increased from 1473 to 1773 K.

decision.trend: Among these references, only PMC10707663 addresses diboride ceramics, describing a liquid precursor route for high-entropy diborides at lower temperatures while achieving high purity and near-single-phase materials. This indicates that advanced processing methods—particularly those enabling densification at reduced temperatures—are gaining traction. Prior efforts used very high temperatures and sometimes multiple components or phases to improve sinterability and mechanical properties, but a direct, single-phase ZrB2 solution has not yet been demonstrated. The key challenge of achieving full density below 2300 °C without altering the stoichiometry remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: How to efficiently produce fully dense, single-phase ZrB2 at lower temperatures without relying on addition of second phases or altering the ceramic’s chemistry. There is also a need for improved strategies to mitigate porosity and resist liquid infiltration during long-term service.
decision.lever: Implement spark plasma sintering (SPS) of high-purity ZrB2 powder at 1800–1900 °C under ~50–80 MPa and rapid heating (~100 °C/min), with a brief dwell (≤10 min) to achieve full densification. The faster heating and applied pressure favor solid-state diffusion and reduce grain growth.
decision.why: SPS has successfully lowered densification temperatures for various refractory ceramics, including diborides, by enhancing diffusion and limiting grain growth. Applying similar parameters to single-phase ZrB2 follows from the trend toward advanced densification methods that reduce processing temperatures, while also mitigating residual porosity that contributes to aqueous infiltration and long-term degradation in service.
